architecture.summary: The claim of a tenant row becomes a lease, and the stop of the tenant loops lets the Render call in flight end: the SO-12 release rehearsal of 31 October 2026 measured that Render keeps the old instance of the control plane for about 120 s after a new deploy is live, and in R9 the old provisioner loop claimed a row 0.4 s after the new loop recorded its service, 81.7 s before the old instance got SIGTERM. Inside the hosted Node server, tenants claims a row for the claim holder of its loop (claimed_by, new at each start) until claimed_until, 60 s later, renews it right before each create and before each read of the deploy, names the holder in each record, frees the row at the end (a creating row only when its lease ends), and leaves a row that another holder holds; app starts the provisioner and the sweeps with a stop signal that ends claims, waits, and new Render calls at once, and an in-flight signal that ends the call in flight 3 s later, inside the hosted deadline of 10 s (FinishingPlatform of tenants, tenant loop of app); a claim that commits during the stop starts no work and frees its row. The data contract of the tenants table gains two columns with a pair check (migration 20261031221342_tenant_claim_lease.sql, applied before the deploy), and the fleet resume records live without a claim. No component, container, public module, dependency, or declaration snapshot changes. The scenario view tenant provisioning changes; the prose of the tenant registry view, the writers of each transition, the deployment view, and the known limits record the lease, the stop, and the residual risk that the sweeps of two instances both run when the daily tick falls inside a deploy.
